    <title>Beyond Discrete Tokens: Preserving Numerical Continuity in Medical Vision-Language Models</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T17:40:58Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32948v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32948v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Objective: To develop a unified vision-language model for prompt-conditioned quantitative ultrasound measurement that addresses the mismatch between continuous measurement targets and discrete token-based numerical prediction. Methods: This article presents HAD-VLM, a hybrid autoregressive-diffusion framework that combines autoregressive text generation with continuous measurement prediction within a shared backbone. Visual prompt tuning adapts the vision encoder to ultrasound images. A diffusion process predicts a five-component representation comprising caliper endpoint coordinates and measurement length. A post-processing strategy combining the proposed coordinate-length consistency mechanism with ensemble prediction is introduced to refine measurement estimates. We evaluate four echocardiographic measurement tasks on EchoNet-LVH, with additional assessments of medical question answering and X-ray vertebral measurement. Results: HAD-VLM achieves mean absolute errors of 1.36, 2.77, 3.05, and 1.16 mm for IVSd, LVIDd, LVIDs, and LVPWd, respectively, reducing errors by 21.4-37.6\% relative to the Vicuna-based autoregressive baseline. It also outperforms fine-tuned Qwen3-VL and direct MLP regression across all four tasks. Medical question answering performance is preserved on the evaluated dataset. For X-ray vertebral measurement, HAD-VLM reduces mean absolute error from 11.4 to 6.7 pixels. Conclusion: Integrating autoregressive language generation with diffusion-based continuous prediction improves quantitative medical image measurement while retaining prompt-conditioned task flexibility. Significance: HAD-VLM provides a unified approach to combining language interaction with anatomically grounded numerical prediction for quantitative medical image analysis.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32946v1</id>
    <title>Low-frustration block encodings by patch routing</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T17:40:02Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32946v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32946v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Block-encoding has emerged as a core primitive in many quantum algorithms, including quantum simulation. In this work, we design efficient and extensible methods for generating low-frustration block encodings of frustrated lattice Hamiltonians built from repeated local interaction patches through a technique we call "patch routing". We construct block encodings for a full Hamiltonian by first block-encoding a small local patch and then using a SWAP-style routing network to coherently apply the local patch encoding across the lattice. The expensive, local block-encoding cost is paid only once per query and is independent of lattice size, whereas the comparatively inexpensive routing network grows linearly with the lattice size, dominating at large sizes. Our method allows for a hierarchical structure in which larger patches can be block-encoded with small normalization factors, albeit at a higher (local, non-extensive) block-encoding cost, thereby reducing overall query complexity in an algorithm. We exploit symmetries and algebraic structures in local interactions to construct efficient block encodings, and we apply these techniques to the Heisenberg, Fermi-Hubbard, and honeycomb spin-liquid models. For a $120\times 120$ square-lattice $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg model near maximal frustration ($J_2/J_1=0.4-0.6$), our methods result in a $15-17\times$ reduction in the leading $T$ cost per qubitized-QPE run (ignoring initial state preparation and overlap) relative to prior state-of-the-art Pauli LCU constructions. Corresponding reductions are approximately $3\times$ for the $120\times120$ Fermi-Hubbard model at half-filling. For time evolution of the honeycomb spin-liquid model on $120\times120$ unit cells, the leading cost is reduced by $5\times$. Our framework provides a systematic way forward for larger and more accurate fault-tolerant simulations of real-world quantum systems.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32945v1</id>
    <title>Monetizing Intelligence: Advertising and Subscription Design on LLM Platforms</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T17:39:42Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32945v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32945v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language model (LLM) platforms introducing advertising must decide how much capability ad revenue should fund and what consumers should pay to avoid ads. We study a monopolistic platform that jointly chooses costly response quality, advertising intensity, and subscription prices when advertising reduces user value but better service raises advertising returns. Three findings follow. First, when partly ad-supported and ad-free plans coexist, advertising can finance useful service for consumers who receive none under pure subscription. Lower effective quality in middle plans weakens the alternatives available to premium users, allowing higher prices for unchanged ad-free service. Some fully ad-supported users gain utility, while partly ad-supported and ad-free users lose: broader access can coexist with utility polarization. Second, an intermediate advertising cap can maximize consumer surplus by preserving some revenue that finances service while limiting degradation. Third, cheaper compute can raise quality and reduce ad intensity, yet sufficiently large cost reductions can increase aggregate advertising revenue above its initial level because better service raises the value of the remaining advertised interactions. An extension shows how advertising-funded upgrades can bring plans to the same maximum capability and advertising exposure, eliminating the basis for different prices. These results make menu design central to evaluating LLM advertising: the consequences extend beyond users who see ads to the alternatives and prices faced by those who do not.</summary>

    <title>Knowledge Distillation across Item and Code Spaces for Parallel Generative Recommendation</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T17:37:55Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32943v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32943v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Generative recommendation with semantic IDs represents each item as a sequence of discrete codes derived from its semantic representation and predicts these codes to generate recommendations. Existing semantic-ID recommenders are typically trained with hard labels for the observed next item. Although such supervision identifies the target, it provides no explicit distributional information about alternative items conditioned on the same user history. Sequential recommenders can supply this item-level predictive knowledge, but transferring it to semantic-ID generation is challenging because the teacher and student operate in item and code spaces, respectively. We propose two complementary knowledge-distillation objectives for parallel semantic-ID recommenders, which predict all code positions simultaneously without autoregressive prefix conditioning. Item Distribution Matching (IDM) reconstructs a catalogue-level item distribution from the student's parallel code predictions and aligns it with the teacher's item distribution. Code Marginal Matching (CMM) projects the teacher's item probabilities onto each code position using fixed item-to-code assignments, then matches the resulting code marginals to the corresponding student heads. Both objectives transfer the teacher's soft distributional knowledge while preserving the student's parallel prediction structure. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that both methods consistently outperform existing state-of-the-art approaches. On average, IDM improves Recall@10 by 15.39%, while CMM improves NDCG@10 by 8.28%. These results demonstrate that distillation in either reconstructed item space or code-marginal space can substantially strengthen hard-label supervision for parallel generative recommendation.</summary>

    <title>If at First You Don't Succeed, Backtrack: Lightweight Recovery for Frozen VLAs</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T17:35:33Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32941v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32941v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models perform well on robotic manipulation, yet remain brittle once their own actions carry them into states their training data barely covers. Recovering from such failures usually requires recovery demonstrations, policy retraining, or a separate model at inference time. We introduce Backtrack, a lightweight failure detection and recovery mechanism for frozen VLAs that needs none of these. A small failure prediction head, trained only on outcome-labeled rollouts of the frozen policy, reads the VLA's existing internal representations to estimate whether the current episode will fail. When the predicted failure probability exceeds a threshold, a controller pauses the policy, retraces the arm's recently achieved motion, and hands control back to the unchanged policy so it can retry from an earlier configuration. The head adds only 0.48-0.88% to the policy's parameter count. We evaluate Backtrack on LIBERO with three VLAs spanning two action-generation families: SmolVLA and $π$0.5, which use flow-matching action experts, and the autoregressive $π$0-FAST. On LIBERO-Long, the suite of long-horizon multi-step tasks and the one on which all three policies fail most often, Backtrack reduces each policy's failure rate by 19-48%, raising success by up to 7.4 percentage points; on the three shorter suites, where control success is already 85-99%, its effect is smaller. On MetaWorld, all twelve controller configurations tested with SmolVLA improve on the unassisted policy.</summary>

    <title>Learning Positive Linear Combinations of ReLUs in Fully Polynomial Time</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T17:34:15Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32940v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32940v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We study the fundamental problem of PAC learning positive linear combinations of $k$ arbitrary ReLU activations on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with respect to the Gaussian distribution, in $L_2$ loss. We give the first fully-polynomial time algorithm for this learning task. Specifically, our algorithm draws $\mathrm{poly}(d, k, 1/ε)$ samples, runs in $\mathrm{poly}(d, k, 1/ε)$ time, and outputs a hypothesis that is $ε$-close to the target concept with high probability. All prior algorithms for this problem require super-polynomial time in $k$ or $1/ε$, or leverage strong well-conditioned assumptions on the weight matrix.
  On a technical level, our approach develops a novel boosting procedure of a ``weak'' learner that recovers the hidden weight vectors to constant error, in a list-decodable manner. To develop this ``weak'' learning procedure, we leverage implicit tensor computation techniques to construct a low-degree filtering procedure based on Hermite tensors of the target function. This procedure amplifies separation among (clusters of) weight vectors to learn each of them to constant error. We then argue that the same procedure can be used for improving the estimation of hidden weight vectors, using gradient descent-like updates on the Euclidean sphere. A crucial ingredient of our algorithm is a pruning approach that ensures only relevant vectors that approximate the hidden weight vectors at target accuracy are maintained by the algorithm.</summary>

    <title>Certain Quantum States Already Require Quantum Time Evolution</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T17:33:33Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32937v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32937v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Model-independent tests of quantum theory, such as Bell inequality violations, focus on static properties of the theory and do not rely on its dynamical aspects. Hence, this core part of quantum theory remains largely untested in a model-independent way. We show that the structure of quantum time evolution can be examined by testing the consistency between the state space and the dynamical laws. Considering a class of generalized phase-space theories, we find that certain quantum states can only be part of a theory if the time evolution is quantum: their evolution in anharmonic potentials would otherwise result in unphysical, negative marginal distributions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the existence of the first excited state of a quantum harmonic oscillator is already sufficient to single out the Moyal bracket (quantum dynamics) to leading order in $\hbar^2$. We outline how theory-independent Wigner tomography of this state can be used to empirically exclude nonquantum dynamical theories.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32936v1</id>
    <title>Generating entanglement in quantum matter with pathway-entangled photons via resonant inelastic X-ray scattering</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T17:32:31Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32936v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32936v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) is conventionally used to probe elementary excitations and correlations in quantum materials. Here, we propose an interferometric RIXS protocol that instead creates entanglement between spatially separated regions of a solid-state material. An incident X-ray photon is coherently split by a beam splitter into two arms illuminating opposite ends of a sample. Recombining the scattered photons at a second beam splitter and detecting an energy-selected photon then projects the material into a coherent superposition of excitations at the two ends. This protocol is the X-ray, solid-state analogue of the Duan-Lukin-Cirac-Zoller (DLCZ) heralding scheme. Using a Kramers-Heisenberg formalism with quantized photon modes, we show that orthogonal and degenerate end excitations yield maximally entangled states. We illustrate this mechanism in three models: (1) two decoupled sites yield a heralded Bell state. (2) An open tight-binding chain exhibits reflection-parity-dependent interference, providing a benchmark for the interferometer's coherence. (3) A spin-1 Haldane (AKLT) chain yields an entangled pair of fractionalized edge spins. We also discuss practical considerations and challenges for realizing the protocol in X-ray experiments.</summary>

    <title>Yalda-Embedding: Open Development of a Competitive Persian Retrieval Model</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T17:30:40Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32933v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32933v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Despite advances in multilingual text representations, effective dense retrieval for Persian remains constrained by the limited availability of language-specific training resources and compact embedding models. We present Yalda Embedding, a 595.8-million-parameter Persian retrieval model adapted from Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B using more than one million query-document pairs. On eight Persian retrieval tasks from FaMTEB, the model achieves the highest macro-average among the evaluated 0.6B models, scoring 0.5488 and outperforming Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B and F2LLM-v2-0.6B on every task. It also approaches Qwen3-Embedding-4B, winning on four tasks, tying on one, and trailing by 0.0075 in macro-average. An incremental ablation study examines contrastive batch size, optimization stabilization, and relational knowledge distillation from F2LLM-v2-8B. Under the one-epoch training setup, contrastive fine-tuning alone yields a modest mean improvement over initialization and regressions on two tasks. The final distilled configuration improves all eight tasks over the non-distilled model, raising the mean from 0.4813 to 0.5488 without increasing inference-time model size. These gains include hard-negative evaluation tasks despite training without explicitly mined or supplied hard negatives. We release model weights, training and evaluation code, the pairwise dataset, and its teacher-embedded counterpart, enabling inspection of data composition and training procedures, independent evaluation, and reuse without repeating expensive teacher inference.</summary>

    <title>ZENO: Nonlinear filtering with Zakai Equation Neural Operators</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T17:24:31Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32926v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32926v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>State inference and parameter learning for nonlinear filters is a core computation for scientific machine learning with varied applications in engineering and neuroscience. The unnormalized filtering distribution is governed by the Zakai equation, a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) that combines the forward Kolmogorov operator (known as the Fokker-Planck equation) with observed likelihood updates. Although solving these high-dimensional SPDEs is often impossible analytically and intractable numerically, advances in operator learning and physics-informed machine learning have made it feasible. Harnessing these advances, we introduce the Zakai Equation Neural Operator (ZENO), a model that optimizes a neural operator against a Zakai Equation based physics-informed loss to approximate the exact unnormalized filtering distribution for latent stochastic dynamical systems. We use this ZENO-inferred posterior distribution in an expectation-maximization (EM) framework to perform parameter learning and state inference. We demonstrate ZENO's ability to accurately infer the posterior distribution and learn its corresponding SDE parameters in three simulated stochastic dynamical systems (Double-Well bistable system, Van Der Pol (VDP) oscillator, and Lorenz system) and compare its performance against established methods for latent SDE inference and learning. We show that ZENO recovers previously observed limit cycles representing forward and backward locomotion from a whole-brain imaging dataset of immobilized \textit{C. elegans} nematodes. ZENO is a novel approach to the problem of nonlinear filtering and dynamical inference through the lens of partial differential equations and operator theory.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32923v1</id>
    <title>One-sided-DIQKD using any pure bipartite entangled state secure against all attacks</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T17:21:46Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32923v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32923v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) allows spatially separated parties to establish a secret key among themselves based on quantum principles. While QKD systems are being deployed worldwide, their reliance on trusted measurements makes them vulnerable. Moreover, existing protocols have largely focussed on the qubit cases, and rely on the maximally entangled state, a costly resource to generate. Here, we consider the one-sided-device-independent (1SDI) QKD protocols, where one of the measurement devices is trusted while the other is untrusted. The resource in this scenario is quantum steering, an asymmetric form of quantum nonlocality. This is inspired by a real-world scenario, where the trusted party can be considered to be a bank, or any large organisation that has sufficient resources to protect its systems and validate them, while the users are vulnerable to attacks. We then demonstrate that a secure key can be obtained using any pure bipartite entangled state in this setup. Considering realistic detectors and sources based on current technology, we demonstrate that even states that are almost separable can be used to extract a secure key. Moreover, for every pure entangled bipartite state, we find the critical detection efficiencies and visibility to obtain a secure key.</summary>

    <title>Adaptive Frequency Threshold Byte Pair Encoding for Mixed Natural Language and Structured Symbolic Corpora</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T17:21:18Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32921v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32921v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Modern language models rely on subwording tokenization to define the discrete units of input processing, typically using methods like Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) that treat whitespace as a fixed semantic boundary. This design is inherently limited, as many meaningful concepts---including multiword expressions and the structured environments of formal languages like LaTeX---frequently span across whitespaces. While recent superword tokenization methods attempt to address this by relaxing whitespace constraints, they often rely on greedy frequency-driven merging that fails to account for token length or the specific needs of underrepresented domain-specific languages. In this paper, we introduce Adaptive Frequency Threshold Byte Pair Encoding (AdaBPE), a new tokenization method that leverages an adaptive frequent-pattern mining approach. AdaBPE features a twofold dynamicity: it adapts minimum frequency thresholds based on both the length of a candidate token, to prevent favoring frequent short patterns, and its type, to distinguish between general and formal language patterns, using LaTeX as case in point. This allows the model to efficiently allocate vocabulary capacity to domain-specific notations, such as LaTeX, even when they represent a small fraction of the training data. We evaluate AdaBPE across five datasets spanning LaTeX and natural language, showing consistent gains in encoding efficiency and downstream language-model performance on domain-specific content without compromising general-language performance.</summary>

    <title>SemantEq: Faithful Bidirectional Equivalence of Formal Statements</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T17:20:12Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32919v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32919v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Statement autoformalization translates mathematics from natural language into a proof assistant such as Lean 4, and models now do it at scale. As provers get stronger, the burden of correctness shifts from the proof to the statement, that is, to whether the formal statement faithfully translates its source. Given a trusted reference formalization, the natural test is logical equivalence, and it proves too much. $P \leftrightarrow Q$ holds trivially for any two statements $P$ and $Q$ that the library proves, because a prover can prove each separately and pass through $P \leftrightarrow \mathrm{True} \leftrightarrow Q$. The stronger the prover, the more unrelated pairs pass. Earlier methods restrict the prover and check that each proof names the other statement. We introduce SemantEq, a more principled relation that instead requires each statement to turn into the other only through a chain of allowed steps, such as logical rearrangement and rewriting with the library's own equations. Our programs judge a proof by the proof term Lean checks, not by its tactic script. SemantEq-Eval, a search without a model, reaches 100% precision and 65.6% recall on the ProofNetVerif test split under our adjudicated labels, against 95.8% and 61.8% for BEq+, and an 8.9-fold increase in its CPU time adds at most three pairs. A language model finds more proofs, but under two of four prompts it proves both directions of about two in five of the non-equivalent pairs. SemantEq-ProofAudit audits each model-written proof under a policy derived from the relation and accepts none of the 104 non-equivalent pairs, and it raises recall on 407 equivalent pairs from 65.4% to 81.1% under the best prompt. Separating the generation of equivalence proofs from their acceptance lets a stronger prover raise recall without changing what an acceptance means. We release code and data at: https://github.com/hlxr89/SemantEq</summary>

    <title>A Tutorial on Physics Constrained Machine Learning for Hybrid Modeling, Optimization, and Control</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T17:17:11Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32914v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32914v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Physics-constrained machine learning (PCML) integrates domain knowledge, first-principles, and physical constraints into AI/ML models. In this work, we present a step-by-step tutorial of a modular PCML framework, KKT-HardNet, and illustrate how it could be used for hybrid modeling, process simulation, optimization and model predictive control in a single platform. KKT-HardNet combines fast inference capabilities of neural networks with guaranteed satisfaction of algebraic constraints through differential projection. It can handle heterogeneous data and enforce both linear and nonlinear equality and inequality constraints. The modular design supports custom neural-network backbones and user-defined projection mechanisms for PCML. To enable efficient end-to-end training, KKT-HardNet exploits implicit function theorem to backpropagate through the projection layer. This avoids computationally expensive automatic differentiation. This work also introduces an exact reduced-order Fischer-Burmeister reformulation and a primal-dual interior-point method as an alternative projection solve strategy. We also provide a diverse set of benchmarking problems for PCML in engineering applications. KKT-HardNet achieves orders of magnitude better performance in terms of both constraint satisfaction and inference time. The KKT-HardNet code and the benchmark datasets are available at https://github.com/souls-tamu/kkt-hardnet .</summary>

    <title>Recommender regret for improving regularised RL estimation with bandits and MCTS</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T17:14:15Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32910v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>Regularised reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms rely on estimators, like Monte Carlo tree search or one-step look-ahead, to provide policy, value, or Q-value estimates in training and inference. However, existing bandit-based estimation frameworks evaluate sampling efficiency, not the quality of estimates. We address this by formalising estimate generation as a recommendation process, treating bandit-based sampling as an improvement operator. To evaluate the quality of a recommendation (estimate), we define regulariser-aware recommender regrets, analysing their lower bounds, and proving that simple algorithms like uniform sampling can achieve these bounds. Finally, we unify bandit- and search-based target improvement under recommender MCTS. Across synthetic trees, arcade games, and scientific discovery tasks, recommenders often yield faster target convergence and superior downstream performance. Our experiments characterise for the first time the potential of regularised MCTS in scientific applications.</summary>

    <summary>Nonclassicality in bosonic systems can be certified directly from occupation probabilities without full state reconstruction. To complete a library of such criteria we introduce a numerical framework that constructs optimal linear nonclassicality witnesses from arbitrary subsets of measured occupation probabilities by solving a semi-infinite linear program. We provide an open-source implementation of the numerical optimization together with the analytical criteria discussed here, enabling direct application of the framework to measured occupation statistics across bosonic platforms.     <title>LoCA: Enabling Multi-Modality in Geospatial Location Encoders</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T17:01:04Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32894v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32894v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Location encoders map geographic coordinates to high-dimensional descriptors through contrastive alignment with paired Earth Observation imagery. We prove that this construction is structurally limited: any Lipschitz location encoder produces an output of intrinsic dimension at most 2, regardless of architecture or bandwidth, which forces the contrastive loss to strictly exceed its asymptotic optimum. Empirically, joint training also collapses the encoder's embedding covariance to low rank. Although dimension-limited, current location encoders sidestep this spectral collapse by training against a frozen image encoder, which we reinterpret as a covariance regularizer that supplies a high-rank target for the location encoder to fold onto. However, extending this approach to multimodal inputs is challenging, as location encoders should simultaneously map a single location to multiple, potentially incompatible, descriptors. We identify two requirements a regularizer must satisfy for location encoding in multimodal regimes: co-alignment across modalities, since adapters alone cannot align independently pretrained encoders; and high effective rank, since the location encoder inherits its target's spectrum. We propose LoCA (Location Contrastive Alignment), a two-stage pipeline that satisfies both. Stage 1 jointly trains Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 encoders with contrastive learning, producing a co-aligned, high-rank multimodal target. Stage 2 freezes the image encoders and trains a location and a tabular metadata encoder as projection adapters with multi-view contrastive learning. Against five state-of-the-art encoders on 17 tasks ranging from land cover and wildfire forecasting to geophysical, socio-economic, biodiversity and climate applications, LoCA achieves the most task wins, is the only model to outperform every other on a majority of tasks, and wins 68.8% of all per-task comparisons.</summary>

    <title>Green Code or Costly Code? Evaluating the Energy Costs of Iterative LLM-Based Code Optimizations</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T16:58:01Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32891v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32891v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to optimize code for performance. This practice often assumes that improvements in execution speed naturally translate into overall lower energy consumption. We challenge this assumption empirically by measuring whether performance-optimized code produced by LLM self-refinement pipelines is also energy-efficient relative to canonical human reference solutions, and whether the energy cost of the optimization process can be offset by subsequent execution-time savings. We evaluate 11 open-source models across four decoding configurations on all 1,000 problems of EffiBench, a state-of-the-art performance benchmark, while collecting per-process, hardware-level energy measurements throughout. Inference energy spans 0.79 to 8.68 MJ across model-variant pairs, which is roughly equivalent to the energy of 250 to 2800 GPT-4.1 queries. Limiting the maximum number of output tokens has the largest impact, reducing energy use by up to 69% compared to the default configuration. On the execution side, 42 of 44 configurations produce code that consumes more energy per problem than the canonical human reference, with overheads ranging from +4% to +886%. The two exceptions achieve only marginal gains, with break-even points on the order of 10^6 to 10^7 executions. Mixture-of-Experts architectures consume substantially less inference energy than equivalently-sized dense models without sacrificing correctness, making architectural choice a more consequential sustainability lever than decoding parameters. Performance optimization and energy efficiency are not always aligned goals: LLM self-refinement consistently produces faster-seeking but energy-heavier code relative to what a human engineer would write. All artifacts are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23598170.</summary>

    <summary>While multimodal contrastive models like CLIP and CLAP successfully learn shared representations, their embeddings typically exhibit a persistent \emph{modality gap}. We propose addressing this separation through a purely geometric approach: changing the embedding domain from the unit sphere, $S^{d-1}$, to the probability simplex, $Δ^{d-1}$. Although both manifolds share the same intrinsic dimension, the simplex acts as a structural prior; its nonnegative, unit-mass constraints serve as a cross-modal calibration that forces both modalities to ground themselves in the same coordinate system. By attaching lightweight softmax adapters and using Total Variation similarity, we reduce the centroid $\ell_2$ gap by 97--99\% across five multimodal retrieval benchmarks. This confirms that simplicial geometry induces genuine semantic alignment, matching or exceeding the retrieval performance of standard unconstrained models.</summary>

    <summary>Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can adapt to local human intervention, while federated learning can combine distributed robot experience without pooling raw records. We examine their prospective intersection: sharing adaptations derived from diverse human corrections across tasks, environments, people, and robot embodiments. Corrections differ in modality, safety semantics(urgency, behavioral scope, etc.), and privacy sensitivity. A shared update that improves mean task success may suppress a rare safety intervention or produce an unsafe response on another robot. We argue for three requirements: preserve the context and uncertainty of multimodal corrections when deciding what to share; assess candidate updates in each receiving robot's closed loop before deployment; and evaluate leakage alongside retention of safety-critical evidence. Immediate, legible defensive behavior remains necessary during human interaction. We offer counterexamples and a falsifiable evaluation agenda, not experimental results.</summary>

    <title>Reinforcement Learning with Multi-Step Transition Predictions: A Bellman Theory</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T16:55:37Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32887v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32887v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multi-step predictions of future transition realizations can improve reinforcement learning, but their value remains difficult to quantify. Directly including these predictions in the state can lead to exponential state-space growth, making direct dynamic programming computationally expensive. We study discounted finite MDPs under a block-feedback protocol: at the start of each K-period block, the decision maker observes $K$-step probabilistic transition predictions for a subset of actions and adapts decisions to observed states within the block. We show that the optimal value satisfies a Bayesian Bellman equation on the original state space. This representation reveals that predictive information creates value by recursively changing the local order of maximization and expectation in the Bellman expansion. We formalize this effect through a Bellman--Jensen analysis and quantify the effects of prediction horizon, error, action coverage, and within-block feedback. We propose block-feedback Bayesian offline learning with online adaptation (BF--BOLA), a model-based algorithm for learning near-optimal policies, and establish upper and lower sample-complexity bounds that match up to logarithmic factors in the stated regimes. The results show that predictions can reduce transition learning to uncovered rows and that learning a near-optimal policy can require fewer prediction samples than estimating the Bayesian value function.</summary>

    <title>Fermion Scattering on Quantum Computers</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T16:48:26Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32882v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32882v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Resonant scattering links particle interactions to the formation and decay of unstable excitations. We develop a hybrid quantum-computing framework to study these dynamics through fermion--antifermion collisions. Our formulation of $(1+1)$-dimensional Yukawa theory encodes fermions in qubits and the scalar field in qumodes. We identify the operations needed for a photonic implementation and benchmark the dynamics with tensor-network simulations. Near resonance, we resolve the build-up of a localised scalar excitation and the subsequent partial return of energy to the fermions. Enhanced entanglement accompanies this exchange. Time-dependent correlator measurements reproduce the analytically predicted decay rate to a few percent precision, with energy scans exhibiting a resonance peak consistent with packet-averaged Breit--Wigner behaviour. These results establish a concrete scattering benchmark for hybrid quantum computers and demonstrate how local real-time observables can probe particle-resonance dynamics.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32881v1</id>
    <title>NgramRL: Accelerating RL Post-Training for Structured Generation via Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T16:47:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32881v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32881v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but its cost is dominated by autoregressive rollout generation, which can exceed 70% of training time. Existing speculative-decoding methods are poorly suited to this setting: model-based drafters consume scarce GPU memory and may become misaligned as the policy evolves, while existing model-free methods do not explicitly exploit repetition across training epochs. We observe that recent rollouts of the same prompt provide a high-quality, self-updating draft source. Based on this insight, we propose NgramRL, a per-prompt n-gram drafter constructed from bounded recent rollout history. NgramRL requires no auxiliary model, drafter training, or persistent GPU-resident drafter state, while target-model verification preserves the rollout distribution. To hide CPU cache lookup and scheduling, we further introduce an adaptive fan-out prefetcher that predicts likely verification outcomes (j, b), consisting of the accepted draft length j and target-emitted continuation token b. A causal budget allocator concentrates prefetches on high-probability outcomes, while uncovered outcomes fall back to sequential lookup without changing committed tokens. Across two model families and three reasoning and structured-generation workloads, NgramRL commits 3.60-7.77 tokens per target-model forward in the warm-cache regime, up to 1.99x more than SuffixDecoding and 7.0x more than prompt-lookup decoding. On Spider, the prefetcher covers 96.6% of Qwen3-8B outcomes at a candidate budget of 16 and improves measured rollout throughput by 1.38x over synchronous NgramRL, approaching its 1.40x overlap ceiling.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32878v1</id>
    <title>Advancing SVD-based LLM Compression via Layer-Wise Error Model Search</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T16:46:00Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32878v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32878v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Low-rank SVD-based compression offers a powerful strategy to reduce the computational costs of LLMs. However, existing methods face two key limitations: (i) global rank allocation, where uncalibrated error proxies fail to capture complex error propagation, and (ii) decomposition quality, where Fisher-based estimators suffer from severe rank collapse. In this work, we address these limitations by introducing Layer-wise Error Modeling Search (LEMS) and KFAC-SVD. LEMS advances rank allocation by introducing a layer-wise error surrogate that integrates local and global layer importance alongside a propagation bias, enabling effective global rank allocation via an ILP formulation. KFAC-SVD improves decomposition quality by utilizing token-wise statistics, mitigating the rank deficiency observed in prior Fisher-based SVD approaches. Across Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama 3 model families, we show that LEMS consistently outperforms existing search strategies, delivering significant zero-shot accuracy gains of up to 4.8 p.p. that generalize to model sizes of 70B parameters, while KFAC-SVD achieves an average perplexity improvement of 15%. Project page and code: https://lems-svd.github.io</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32876v1</id>
    <title>Trusting the Tool: Asymmetric Deference of LLM Vulnerability Auditors to Static-Analysis Evidence</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T16:45:10Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32876v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32876v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Pipelines that combine large language models (LLMs) with static analysis let the model consume the analyser's output as evidence, but whether the model distinguishes true from false evidence, and whether its scrutiny depends on what the evidence claims, has not been measured. We built an intraprocedural analyser for C/C++ that produces proof obligations and audited vulnerable and patched functions from PrimeVul under six evidence conditions that differ only in the notes, including fabricated assurances that a missing check exists and fabricated alarms that an added check is missing. The study covers 916 pairs in four disjoint sets, eleven model configurations from four vendors and 16,572 audits; no model is trained or fine-tuned. True evidence barely improved accuracy (+0.02). False evidence acted asymmetrically: relative to true notes about the same operations, false assurances lowered the detection of real vulnerabilities by up to 19 points, whereas false alarms never significantly lowered accuracy and were disputed far more often. An internally registered replication on seven new models confirmed that false assurances move verdicts towards their claim more than false alarms do (mean asymmetry +0.16, 95% CI +0.10 to +0.24). Instructions in the audit prompt did not reliably reduce deference; the best one failed to replicate. Verifying each claim in a separate call and showing the refuted claims raised accuracy under false assurances by 12 points in a pre-specified test (p=0.002) without loss under true evidence; for a second model the gain was smaller and not significant. Pipelines should therefore verify a tool's guarantees before the model relies on them, and studies should measure deference in a direction-aware way.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32874v1</id>
    <title>Do "True" and "False" Add Up to One? Complement Consistency in LLM-Agent Opinion Simulations</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T16:44:20Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32874v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32874v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In LLM-agent opinion simulations, each agent reports the probability that a claim is true after seeing its own previous probability and the probabilities reported by its neighbors, and that number becomes its state in the next round. If the number describes the agent's position rather than the sentence it was shown, then rewriting the claim as its complement and replacing every probability p with 1 - p should return the complementary answer, so the two reports should sum to one. We test this with three small open models: Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.2-3B and Gemma-3-4B. On 2,304 agent states taken from a running network simulation, Qwen's paired reports sum to 1.18 on average, and on 48 real fact-checking claims from AVeriTeC they again exceed one. A controlled benchmark of 24 worlds, each with exactly two possible outcomes, shows the same failure in all three models. The discrepancy is two to ten times larger than the change produced by a same-meaning paraphrase, and it persists under repeated sampling and across peer group sizes and report strengths. When the reports are fed back into two populations that start from complementary states, the populations do not remain mirror images: their divergence is positive after five rounds for every model. Averaging each answer with the complement of its paired answer restores consistency by construction and lowers Brier loss averaged over the two wordings, but at the final round it beats the better of the two original wordings for only one of the three models. A schedule-by-targeting experiment on the same model gives a small, stable interaction because such sweeps keep the claim wording fixed. Consistency under rewording therefore needs its own test before simulated probabilities are read as beliefs</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32869v1</id>
    <title>From Deliberately Constructed Systemic Representations of the World of Activity to Dialogue: A Five-Level Communication Architecture for Strong Language-Based ASI</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T16:41:54Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32869v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32869v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>This paper proposes a five-level organization of message formation and understanding within thinking and activity in which ASI participates. Its central thesis is that a language model's context is fundamentally incapable of presenting the foundations of utterance formation for examination and verification. These foundations are established in advance by acquired schemas, systemic representations of the world of activity, and connections accepted as true within them. Neither context nor trained LLM weights, in themselves, attest to the presence of deliberately constructed systemic representations. The five levels distinguish systemic representations of the world of activity, a particular situation cut out from those representations, its narrative description, the full sense of a message, and text. A situation's schema-model is not identical to a story about it. A recipient reconstructs the full sense from an abbreviated text through jointly constructed and agreed-upon representations and joint activity. Reverse work proceeds from the full sense through an extended description and the situation's schema-model to the reconstruction of systemic foundations. The theoretical foundations draw on the systems methodology of G. P. Shchedrovitskiy, the structural differential of A. Korzybski, and the Meaning-Text theory of I. A. Mel'chuk. The contribution is a specific systemic-activity organization of content for examining and adjusting message foundations and controlling the consequences of their transformation. Further research concerns large graphical models of activity on reconstructible systemic foundations, distinct from text generation from context.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32866v1</id>
    <title>Interpretable sparse fine-tuning with TopKLoRA enables faithful circuit discovery</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T16:37:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32866v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32866v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Fine-tuning on datasets of unknown origin can create a backdoor in the trained model when the data includes poisoned examples. Difficult to localise and remove, backdoors can persist through safety training. While parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods capture the full parameter changes introduced during training, they are not easily interpretable. We present the full method of TopKLoRA, extending the preliminary proposal of Masiak et al. (2025), an interpretable-by-design LoRA variant in which only the $k$ largest adapter latents are active at each token. Unlike SAEs, TopKLoRA is trained purely on downstream loss, where optimisation pressure incentivises learning functionally causal latents. We demonstrate this sparse LoRA adapter in a sleeper-agent backdoor case study where we create model organisms by fine-tuning gemma-2-2b, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and Qwen2.5-7B on a poisoned instruction-following dataset. For each organism, we identify and ablate a circuit that is both necessary and sufficient to implement the backdoor. Furthermore, our new fine-tuning method produces sparse circuits that are up to an order of magnitude smaller than a dense LoRA baseline, allowing surgical ablation of the malicious capability without sacrificing instruction-following performance. Finally, we propose a technique to construct model organisms with localised circuits using TopKLoRA latents and gradient-routing, which we use to validate the findings of our circuit search algorithm. We consider these findings as a step toward interpretable-by-design architectures that provide faithful units of analysis without compromising model performance. We share our code: https://github.com/interpretable-finetuning/TopKLoRA.</summary>

    <title>PoKER: A Probability of Kill Estimation Rate Model for Air-to-Air Missiles Using Machine Learning on Stochastic Targets</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T16:34:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32864v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32864v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>This work introduces PoKER, a novel probabilistic model engineered to optimize missile launch effectiveness in air-to-air scenarios, specifically within Beyond Visual Range (BVR) air combat. Unlike conventional Weapon Engagement Zone (WEZ) models that delineate zones based on static distances such as maximum, minimum, and no-escape ranges, PoKER applies machine learning to predict kill probabilities more accurately by integrating the stochastic behaviors of targets and missile miss distances. This model dynamically evaluates target behavior, greatly expanding the predictive capabilities of engagement analysis. By factoring in elements such as warhead lethality, target and shooter orientations, and the specific conditions of engagement, PoKER provides important insights into engagement dynamics and quantifies success probabilities. Consequently, it can potentially be an important tool for BVR air combat pilots, improving operational decision-making within this specialized combat domain.</summary>

    <title>A Foundation Model for Policy In-Context Longitudinal Causal Effect Estimation</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T16:34:49Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32863v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32863v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Longitudinal causal effect estimation is complicated by time-varying confounding and treatment-confounder feedback loops. Existing methods generally require data-specific nuisance-model fitting, and many are tailored to prespecified treatment sequences or prediction horizons, leading to time-consuming computation at deployment. We introduce *Policy In-Context Longitudinal causal Effect estimation with Prior-data Fitted Networks* (**PICLE-PFN**), the first foundation model for longitudinal causal effect estimation that supports *dynamic* treatment policies. PICLE-PFN represents target policies through in-context history-decision demonstrations, providing a unified interface for a broad class of treatment policies. Pretrained over synthetic data sampled from longitudinal structural causal models, PICLE-PFN amortizes causal effect estimation across datasets, policies, and horizons. Given a new observational dataset and target policy, it directly predicts conditional average potential outcomes (CAPOs) in one forward pass without task-specific training or hyperparameter tuning. Across synthetic and semi-synthetic longitudinal benchmarks, PICLE-PFN achieves competitive RMSE and substantially improved uncertainty calibration with a fraction of deployment runtime, compared to state-of-the-art conventional estimators trained and tuned separately for each dataset.</summary>

    <title>Sustainability of TSFM Deployment and Pretraining: From Carbon Footprint Analysis to Mitigation via Pruning</title>
    <updated>2026-10-23T16:32:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32859v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.32859v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) offer strong zero-shot forecasting capabilities, but their high pretraining cost raises a practical sustainability question: does this upfront investment pay off over a full deployment lifecycle, compared to supervised standalone models that must be periodically retrained? We model the cumulative carbon cost of different approaches across a realistic industrial scenario: Chronos-2 amortizes its pretraining cost within months for large or frequently queried deployments, but a classical model remains cheaper indefinitely for small or rarely queried ones. For cases where reducing the TSFM's own cost matters, we show that removing a single encoder block (7.9% of parameters) via a gradient-free pruning criterion yields a consistent 6 to 9% reduction in FLOPs, CO2 emissions, and latency, at essentially no cost to zero-shot forecasting performance across a 25-task benchmark.</summary>

assessed up to approximately 12 months"}]},"eligibilityModule":{"eligibilityCriteria":"Inclusion Criteria:

* Adults (aged ≥ 18 years)
* Histologically confirmed diagnosis of a non-Hodgkin or Hodgkin lymphoma that has progressed in spite of prior treatment, and for which additional effective standard therapy is not available
* Patients may have either measurable or non-measurable disease, but in all cases eligible patients must have disease that can be clinically evaluated for improvement or progression
* Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status ≤2
* Adequate hematological, renal, hepatic, and coagulation laboratory assessments
* Written informed consent to participate in this study before the performance of any study-related procedure

Exclusion Criteria:

* A primary lymphoma of the central nervous system (CNS) or known lymphomatous involvement of the CNS. CNS imaging and cerebrospinal fluid sampling are not mandatory in the absence of a clinical suspicion of lymphomatous involvement of the CNS.
* Current infection with HIV, Hepatitis B or Hepatitis C. Patients will have serologic testing performed during screening for HIV and Hepatitis B and C. Any serologic results suggestive of an ongoing viral infection will be further investigated as necessary to clarify the patient's status.
* Impairment of gastrointestinal (GI) function or GI disease that may significantly alter the absorption of CPI-0610, including any unresolved nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea that is CTCAE grade \>1.
* Impaired cardiac function or clinically significant cardiac diseases, including any of the following:

  * Acute myocardial infarction or angina pectoris ≤ 6 months prior to starting study drug
  * Serum cardiac troponin (cTn) level ≥ 99% percentile of the upper reference limit
  * QTcF \> 470 msec on the screening ECG
  * Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) \< 40%
* Uncontrolled cardiac arrhythmia (patients with rate-controlled atrial fibrillation are not excluded.)
* Any other concurrent severe and/or uncontrolled concomitant medical condition that could compromise participation in the study (e.g., clinically significant pulmonary disease, clinically significant neurological disorder, active or uncontrolled infection)
* Systemic anti-cancer treatment or radiotherapy less than 2 weeks before the first dose of CPI-0610
* Radioimmunotherapy (e.g., 131I-tositumomab, 90Y-ibritumomab tiuxetan) less than 6 weeks before the first dose of CPI-0610
* Treatment with an investigational small molecule less than 2 weeks before the first dose of CPI-0610. In addition, the first dose of CPI-0610 should not occur before a period equal to or greater than 5 half-lives of the small molecule investigational agent has elapsed.
* Treatment with a therapeutic antibody less than 4 weeks before the first dose of CPI-0610. A minimum 2-week period between the last treatment with a therapeutic antibody and the first dose of CPI-0610 may be permitted in patients with rapidly progressive or aggressive subtypes of lymphoma following discussion with the medical monitor.
* Treatment with medications that are known to be strong inhibitors or inducers of CYP450 enzymes.
* Treatment with medications that are known to carry a risk of Torsades de Pointes.
* Immunosuppressive treatment that cannot be discontinued both prior to study entry and for the duration of the study. Oral prednisone at a dose of 10 mg or less per day is allowed, as are other oral corticosteroids given at glucocorticoid-equivalent doses. Topical, nasal and inhaled corticosteroids are also allowed.
* Pregnant or lactating women
* Women of child-bearing potential and men with reproductive potential, if they are unwilling to use adequate contraception while on study therapy and for 3 months thereafter

* Extranodal NK/T cell lymphoma, nasal type
* Age 18-60 years at time of randomization
* Life expectancy of 3 months or longer
* ECOG performance status (PS) 0, 1 or 2 at the time of randomization. However, PS 3 will be acceptable if lymphoma-related.
* Measurable disease (defined as at least one lesion with two measurable perpendicular diameters of which at least one should be \>= 15 mm).
* Written informed consent

* Precursor T cell lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia

* Alk-positive and negative anaplastic large cell lymphoma
* Blastic NK cell lymphoma
* Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, transformed or not
* Concurrent severe and/or uncontrolled medical disease (e.g. uncontrolled diabetes, congestive heart failure, myocardial infarction within 6 months prior to the study, unstable and uncontrolled hypertension, chronic renal disease, or active uncontrolled infection), which could compromise participation in the study.

* Severe cardiac dysfunction (NYHA classification II-IV, Appendix H) or LVEF \< 45 %

* History of active cancer during the past 5 years, except basal carcinoma of the skin or stage 0 cervical carcinoma
* Unwillingness or inability to comply with the protocol
* Simultaneous participation in any other study protocol

1. Patients aged 18-75 years.
2. Subjects with histologically or cytologically-documented locally advanced NSCLC who present with stage IVA or IVB according to the 8th TNM classification. Pathological characterization must be sufficient to define patients as having either squamous or non-squamous histology.
3. Previous treatment/s for NSCLC with platinum-based 1st line therapy regimen with or without maintainance therapy and documented disease progression. First line platinum-based therapy has to consist of at least 4 cycles.
4. Patients with a known sensitizing mutation in the EGFR gene must have experienced disease progression (during or after treatment) or intolerance to treatment with afatinib, erlotinib, gefitinib, or another EGFR-TKI approved for the treatment of EGFR-mutant NSCLC. Patients with a known ALK fusion oncogene must have experienced disease progression (during or after treatment) or intolerance to treatment with crizotinib or another ALK-TKI approved for the treatment of NSCLC in patients having an ALK fusion oncogene.
5. Evaluable tumor tissue available (either FFPE tissue block or unstained tumor tissue section); fresh or archival.
6. Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) Performance Status (PS) 0 or 1.
7. Patients must have at least one unidimensionally measurable lesion by computed tomography or MRIas defined by RECIST criteria 1.1.
8. Prior radiation therapy is allowed, if the irradiated area is not the only source of measurable or assessable disease and if the radiation therapy is not within 4 weeks of the administration of study treatment.
9. All acute toxic effects (excluding alopecia and fatigue) of any prior therapy (including surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy) must have resolved to National Cancer Institute (NCI) Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) (v4.03) Grade ≤ 1.
10. All baseline laboratory requirements will be assessed and should be obtained within 21 days of treatment start. Screening laboratory values must meet the following criteria:

    * Absolute neutrophil count (ANC) ≥ 1.0 x 109/L, platelets ≥ 100 x 109/L, haemoglobin (Hb) ≥ 9.0 g/dl.
    * Alkaline phosphatase (ALP), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and or aspartate aminotransferase (AST) ≤ 3 x upper limit of reference range (ULN), and total bilirubin ≤ 2.0 mg/L unless liver involvement by the tumor, in which case the transaminase levels could be ≤ 5 x ULN.
    * Creatinine ≤ 1.5 ULN or creatinine clearance ≥ 30 mL/min.
11. Estimated life expectancy of at least 12 weeks.
12. Negative serum pregnancy test for females of childbearing potential\*.
13. Documented negative test for HIV, HBV and HCV. For HBV serology: the determination of HBsAg, anti-HBsAg-Ab and anti-HBcAg-Ab is required. In patients with serology documenting previous exposure to HBV (i.e., anti-HBsAb with no history of vaccination and/or anti-HBcAb), negative serum HBV-DNA is required. For HCV: HCV RNA or HCV antibody test. Subjects with a positive tst for HCV antibody but no detection of HCV RNA indicating no current infection are eligible.
14. Negative TB test (e.g. Mantoux or Quantiferon assay)
15. Written informed consent.

    * Subjects or legal rappresentative must have signed and dated an IRB/IEC approved written informed consent form in accordance with regulatory and institutional guidelines. This must be obtained before the performance of any protocol related procedures that are not part of normal subject care.
    * Subjects must be willing and able to comply with scheduled visits, treatment schedule, laboratory tests and other requirements of the study.

      * Women of childbearing potential (WOCBP) must be using, from the screening to six months following the last study drug administration, highly effective contraception methods, as defined by the "Recommendations for contraception and pregnancy testing in clinical trials" issued by the Head of Medicine Agencies' Clinical Trial Facilitation Group (www.hma.eu/ctfg.html) and which include, for instance, progesteron-only or combined (estrogen- and progesteron-containing) hormonal contraception associated with inhibition of ovulation, intrauterine devices, intrauterine hormone-releasing systems, bilateral tubal occlusion or vasectomised partner. Pregnancy test will be repeated at the end of treatment visit.

Women of childbearing potential are defined as females who have experienced menarche, are not postmenopausal (12 months with no menses without an alternative medical cause) and are not permanently sterilised (e.g., tubal occlusion, hysterectomy, bilateral oophorectomy or bilateral salpingectomy).

Exclusion Criteria:

a. Cancer-specific exclusions

1. Any tumor therapy (chemotherapy, biologics for cancer, or an investigational therapy) within 4 weeks of the administration of study treatment.
2. Uncontrolled tumor-related pain; patients requiring pain medication must be on a stable regimen at study entry. Symptomatic lesions amenable to palliative radiotherapy (e.g., bone metastases or metastases causing nerve impingement) should be treated prior to enrollment.
3. Active symptomatic central nervous system metastases. Subjects are eligible if CNS metastases have been treated and subjects have neurologically returned to baseline (except for residual signs or symptoms related to the CNS treatment) for at least 4 weeks prior to the first administration of study treatment.
4. Subjects must have been either off corticosteroids, or on a stable or decreasing dose ≤ 10 mg daily prednisone (or equivalent) for at least 2 weeks prior to enrollment.
5. Carcinomatous meningitis

   b. General Medical Exclusions
6. Previous or concurrent cancer that is distinct in primary site or histology from the cancer being evaluated in this study or any cancer curatively treated \< 5 years prior to study entry, except cervical carcinoma in situ, non-melanoma skin cancer, superficial bladder tumors.
7. Pregnant and lactating women.
8. Uncontrolled medical condition considered as high risk for the treatment with an investigational drug (e.g. unstable diabetes mellitus, vena-cava-syndrome, uncontrolled pleural effusion, pericardial effusion).
9. Prior allogeneic bone marrow transplantation or solid organ transplant.
10. Heart failure (\> Grade II, New York Heart Association Criteria - NYHA).
11. History within the last 12 months of acute or subacute coronary syndromes including myocardial infarction, unstable or severe stable angina pectoris.
12. Irreversible cardiac arrhythmias requiring permanent medication.
13. History of stroke or transient ischemic attack within the previous 12 months.
14. Severe or uncontrolled hypertension according to WHO criteria.
15. Ischemic peripheral vascular disease (Grade IIb-IV).
16. Documented history or active autoimmune disorders with the exception of:
17. skin disorders (such as vitiligo, psoriasis, or alopecia),
18. stable diabetes mellitus type 1,
19. Autoimmune thyroiditis requiring hormone replacement only.
20. Presence of primary or secondary immune deficiency.
21. Major trauma including surgery (such as abdominal/cardiac/thoracic surgery) within 4 weeks of administration of study treatment.
22. Known history of allergy to IL-2 or other intravenously administered human proteins/peptides/antibodies.
23. Neuropathy \> Grade 2.
24. Presence of active and uncontrolled infections or other severe concurrent disease, which, in the opinion of the investigator, would place the patient at undue risk or interfere with the study.
25. Subject unlikely to comply with protocol, e.g. uncooperative attitude, inability to return for follow-up visits, and unlikelihood of completing the study.
26. Any severe concomitant condition which makes it undesirable for the patient to participate in the study or which could jeopardize compliance with the protocol.

    c. Exclusion criteria related to medication
27. Treatment with any investigational study drug within 4 weeks before beginning of study treatment.
28. Treatment with hematopoietic growth factors or immunomodulatory agents within 7 days of the administration of study treatment.
29. Immunosuppressive treatment within 2 weeks prior to cycle 1, day 1.
30. Any condition requiring systemic treatment with either corticosteroids (\> 10 mg daily prednisone equivalent) or other immunosuppressive medications within 14 days prior to start of study drug (inhaled steroids and adrenal replacement steroid doses are permitted in absence of any active autoimmune disease)
31. Prior therapy with anti-PD-1, anti-PD-L1, anti-PD-L2, anti-CD137, or anti-CTLA-4 antibody (or any other antibody or drug specifically targeting T-cell co-stimulation or checkpoint pathways).
32. Interstitial lung disease that is symptomatic or may interfere with the detection or management of suspected drug-related pulmonary toxicity
33. Patient randomized to one of the treatment arms described below.

RegimenI(Standard treatment: dd-TCiv therapy): Paclitaxel administered by IV infusion weekly plus concurrent carboplatin administered by IV infusion once every 3 weeks

RegimenII(Study treatment: dd-TCip therapy): Paclitaxel administered by IV infusion weekly plus concurrent carboplatin administered by IP injection once every 3 weeks

The 3-week period (21 days) is 1 cycle. Protocol treatment basically comprises 6 cycles. IDS is allowed to be performed after 3, 4 or 5 cycles of the protocol treatment. In such cases, the protocol treatment must be restarted within 8 weeks after IDS. If IDS is performed, patients can receive up to 3 additional cycles of the protocol treatment after IDS. If interval debulking surgery (IDS) is performed after 3, 4 or 5 cycles, the patients can receive up to 3 additional cycles of the protocol treatment. A total of 6 to 8 cycles will be repeated.

The analysis of efficacy will be performed on all randomized subjects in accordance with the intention-to-treat (ITT) principle. In order to assess the robustness of the results, the same analyses will be done using all randomized subjects who satisfy the eligibility criteria.    * Electrocardiogram (ECG): Patients with normal ECG, Asymptomatic patients with abnormal ECGs not requiring medical intervention

8. Patients aged 20 years and older at the time of tentative registration (with no upper age limit)
9. Patients who provide written informed consent for participation in this trial

1. Patients assumed to have a borderline malignancy of the ovary, fallopian tube, or primary peritoneal cancer

randomization)"}]},"eligibilityModule":{"eligibilityCriteria":"Inclusion Criteria:

* Have pathologically confirmed de novo DLBCL or DLBCL transformed from previously diagnosed indolent lymphoma (e.g., follicular lymphoma). Patient with high-grade lymphoma with c-MYC, Bcl2 and/or Bcl6 rearrangements are eligible (only for Phase 2). (Documentation to be provided).
* Have received at least 1 but no more than 3 prior lines of systemic therapy for the treatment of DLBCL with relapsed or refractory disease following their most recent regimen.

  * Salvage chemoimmunotherapy followed by stem cell transplantation will be considered as 1 line of systemic therapy.
  * Maintenance therapy will not be counted as a separate line of systemic therapy.
  * Radiation with curative intent for localized DLBCL will not be counted as 1 line of systemic therapy.
* Positron emission tomography (PET) positive measurable disease with at least 1 node having the longest diameter (LDi) greater than (\>) 1.5 centimeter (cm) or 1 extranodal lesion with LDi \>1 cm (per the Lugano Criteria 2014). The Deauville 5-point scale (D5PS) score assessed on the FDG PET/CT should be between 3 to 5.
* Not intended for HSCT or CAR-T cell therapy based on objective clinical criteria determined by the treating physician. Patients who cannot receive HSCT due to active disease are allowed on study (up to approximately 15 percent \[%\] of patients enrolled in each Phase). Documentation on lack of intention to proceed to receive HSCT or CAR-T therapy must be provided by the treating physician.
* Adequate bone marrow function at screening, defined as:

  * Absolute neutrophil count (ANC) ≥1\*10\^9 per liter (/L).
  * Platelet count ≥100\*10\^9/L (without platelet transfusion less than \[\<\] 14 days prior to Cycle 1 Day 1 \[C1D1\]).
  * Hemoglobin ≥8.5 gram per deciliter (g/dL) (without red blood cell transfusion \<14 days prior to C1D1).
* Circulating lymphocytes less than or equal to (≤) 50\*10\^9/L.
* Adequate liver and kidney function, defined as:

  * Aspartate transaminase (AST) or alanine transaminase (ALT) ≤2.5\*upper limit of normal (ULN), or ≤5\*ULN in cases with known lymphoma involvement in the liver.
  * Serum total bilirubin ≤2\*ULN, or ≤5\*ULN if due to Gilbert syndrome or in cases with known lymphoma involvement in the liver.
  * Calculated creatinine clearance (CrCl) ≥30 milliliter per minute (mL/min) based on Cockcroft-Gault formula.
* Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of ≤2.
* An estimated life expectancy of \>3 months at Screening.
* Patients with primary refractory DLBCL defined as no response or relapse within 6 months after ending first-line treatment, will be allowed in the study.
* Agree to highly effective contraception during the duration of the study with contraception use continuing for 12 months after the last dose of study treatment
* Female patients of childbearing potential must have a negative serum pregnancy test at Screening and agree to use highly effective methods of contraception throughout the study and for 12 months following the last dose of study treatment (except patients with Non-Childbearing potential: Age \>50 years and naturally amenorrhoeic for \>1 year, or previous bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, or hysterectomy).
* Male patients who are sexually active must use highly effective methods of contraception throughout the study and for 12 months following the last dose of study treatment. Male patients must agree not to donate sperm during the study treatment period and for 12 months following the last dose of study treatment.

Exclusion Criteria:

* DLBCL with mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma, composite lymphoma (Hodgkin's lymphoma + non-Hodgkin's lymphoma \[NHL\]), DLBCL transformed from diseases other than indolent NHL; primary mediastinal (thymic) large B-cell lymphoma (PMBL); T-cell rich large B-cell lymphoma.
* Previous treatment with selinexor or other XPO1 inhibitors.
* Contraindication to any drug contained in the combination therapy regimen (SR-GDP).
* Known active central nervous system or meningeal involvement by DLBCL at time of Screening.
* Use of any standard or experimental anti-DLBCL therapy (including nonpalliative radiation, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, radio-immunotherapy, or any other anticancer therapy) \<21 days prior to C1D1 (prednisone \<30 mg or equivalent is permitted; palliative radiation is permitted only if on non-target lesions).
* Any AE, by C1D1, which has not recovered to Grade ≤1 (Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events \[CTCAE\], v.5.0), or returned to baseline, related to the previous DLBCL therapy, except hematological abnormalities (as specified in the inclusion criteria) and alopecia.
* Major surgery \<14 days of Cycle 1 Day 1.
* Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation/CAR-T therapy as follows:
